item.title: Analysis: AI companies are not being charged with hacking despite concerns over their data practices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The article explores why AI companies have not faced legal charges for activities that some consider hacking, focusing on the complexities of applying existing laws to AI data usage. It discusses the challenges in defining unauthorized access and the legal ambiguities surrounding AI training data collection. The piece highlights the tension between innovation in AI development and the enforcement of cybersecurity laws, noting that current regulations may not adequately address the nuances of AI-related data practices. It also considers the implications for privacy, intellectual property, and future regulatory approaches as AI technologies continue to evolve.

item.title: QGIS bans AI-assisted contributions citing maintainers' workload and community trust concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: QGIS has implemented a strict ban on AI-assisted contributions to its project, citing the increased pressure on maintainers and the risk of quality issues from unreviewed AI-generated code. The decision aims to protect the human-centered nature of the open-source community and ensure contributors develop skills through genuine engagement. The policy change follows discussions highlighting that AI-generated contributions can overwhelm reviewers and potentially degrade code quality. Some contributors expressed concerns that reliance on AI tools hinders learning and community growth. The QGIS team plans to separately explore the use of AI for code review, auditing, and security in future discussions.

item.title: Andrej Karpathy says understanding of large language model capabilities is diverging sharply among different user groups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Andrej Karpathy highlights a widening gap in how different groups perceive and use large language models (LLMs). He categorizes users into four groups: about 6 billion people with little to no exposure, 1-2 billion casual users who see LLMs as basic tools, around 20 million professionals using advanced LLMs for complex coding tasks, and roughly 5,000 insiders with access to frontier-grade systems enabling large-scale, rapid projects. This divergence stems from differences in access, use cases, and the complexity of problems tackled by LLMs. Karpathy explains that the impact of LLMs scales with the ambition and complexity of tasks, with capabilities peaking in digital, verifiable, and economically valuable domains like math and coding. He notes that while most people experience LLMs as simple chatbots, a small group is witnessing transformative changes in software development and scientific research. This creates a sharp funnel of understanding and experience that is growing as LLM technology advances rapidly.

item.title: Veda launches first hobby OS with built-in AI agent integrated at the kernel level, running on x86-64 and QEMU [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Veda has introduced a hobby operating system built from scratch in Rust that integrates an AI agent directly into the OS kernel, enabling users to control native system services via natural-language commands. The OS supports over 70 built-in actions and uses Deepgram's Voice Agent platform for speech recognition and synthesis. It runs on x86-64 hardware and QEMU, with a public beta available on GitHub. This approach challenges traditional SaaS models by embedding AI functionality at the OS layer rather than as an add-on, potentially reducing latency and improving reliability. Veda's open-source OS could serve as a foundation for AI-native products and vertical SaaS solutions that leverage deep system integration to differentiate in competitive markets. The company aims to address scalability and enterprise integration challenges to expand beyond hobbyist use.

item.title: Report: AI technologies are fueling a scam economy that now exceeds the global cocaine trade in scale [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to enhance scam operations, leading to a significant expansion of fraudulent activities worldwide. This growth has created a scam economy that surpasses the size of the global cocaine trade, posing new challenges for law enforcement and regulatory agencies. The use of AI enables scammers to automate and scale their efforts more efficiently, making detection and prevention more difficult. Authorities are struggling to keep pace with these AI-driven scams, which are evolving rapidly and affecting a broad range of victims across different sectors.

item.title: Sources: OpenAI in talks with stealth startup co-founded by Jeffrey Katzenberg to revive and commercialize Sora video model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI is reportedly negotiating with a stealth startup co-founded by Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg, former Sora research lead Bill Peebles, and ex-Dropbox CFO Sujay Jaswa to access and modify its discontinued video model Sora for filmmaking applications. The original Sora model and its TikTok-like app were shelved earlier this year amid OpenAI's broader cutbacks on server-intensive side projects, even as competitors like xAI and Google advanced their own video AI models. The startup, whose name remains undisclosed, aims to leverage Sora's technology to develop software or services for filmmakers, potentially bringing the model back into active use after its initial cancellation. This move reflects ongoing interest in AI-driven video generation despite OpenAI's earlier decision to halt Sora's development.

item.title: Microsoft debuts Maia 300 AI chip and plans multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027 [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Microsoft announced its latest homegrown AI chip, the Maia 300, and revealed plans to deploy it at multi-gigawatt scale beginning next year. This initiative aims to reduce the company's reliance on Nvidia-designed GPUs for AI workloads. The move reflects Microsoft's strategy to expand its in-house hardware capabilities to support growing AI demands.

item.title: Microsoft President Brad Smith says UK is best positioned to lead global AI regulation amid calls for urgent safety rules
item.description: Microsoft President Brad Smith called for urgent regulation of artificial intelligence, highlighting that AI companies currently face less oversight than industries like dairy and home appliances. He identified the United Kingdom as best placed to lead global AI safety efforts due to its AI Security Institute's access to major AI models and its emerging leadership in AI safety testing. Smith noted that despite pushback from the U.S., including President Donald Trump's warnings against globalist interference, the UK can regulate AI in ways the U.S. cannot, partly because Washington views the UK differently than Brussels. He advocated for legal obligations such as breach notifications, external approvals before AI product releases, and kill-switch mechanisms to manage AI risks, emphasizing that voluntary self-regulation is insufficient to address irresponsible actors in the AI industry.

item.title: Blueprints AI launches software that generates permit-ready construction blueprints from sketches or PDFs in minutes [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Blueprints AI, a Santa Monica startup, has developed software that uses AI to create code-compliant, permit-ready architectural blueprints quickly from inputs like photos, PDFs, or sketches. The company says its technology can produce these blueprints within minutes, aiming to reduce the time architects spend on drafting and increase their focus on design. Founded by architect Al Drams and data scientist Coco Cao, Blueprints AI trained its models on eight years of approved drawing sets from Drams' architecture and construction firm. The startup recently released a second-generation version that allows users to design and update entire building projects-including architecture, structural, mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and interior design-with changes automatically checked against local building codes. Licensed architects still review and seal the documents before permit submission, maintaining professional oversight.

item.title: Amaiko CTO details cost savings after AI agents began handling infrastructure and code tasks, reducing monthly expenses to about €1,500 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Amaiko's engineering team of three merged 708 pull requests in four weeks while relying on AI agents Claude and Codex to manage most operational tasks such as Kubernetes upgrades, CI runners, log triage, and code review. This shift allowed the company to reduce infrastructure and tooling costs to approximately €1,500 per month at list prices, significantly lowering expenses compared to traditional cloud providers. The team rents 16 Hetzner Cloud servers running Kubernetes clusters and various services, with AI agents performing hands-on work under human supervision. Compared to AWS, Hetzner's setup is roughly five to eight times cheaper on demand. Monitoring is handled internally with Prometheus, Grafana, and related tools, replacing previous solutions and further optimizing costs. The entire infrastructure is managed as code, enabling quick migration if needed.

item.title: Microsoft's Office chief Charles Lamanna proposed using Anthropic AI models to improve Copilot amid 2025 customer complaints [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: In mid-2025, Microsoft faced customer dissatisfaction with its AI assistant Copilot, which struggled to automate tasks in Excel and PowerPoint. Charles Lamanna, then a Microsoft president, suggested to CEO Satya Nadella that the company should consider paying for AI models from Anthropic to enhance Copilot's performance, a proposal that was initially controversial within the company. Lamanna described the idea as "heresy" at the time, indicating internal resistance to outsourcing AI capabilities. His initiative marked a significant shift in Microsoft's approach to improving its AI tools by leveraging external technology to address product shortcomings.

item.title: OpenCode releases migration guide for upgrading from version 1 to version 2 with breaking changes and configuration updates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenCode has published a detailed migration guide for users upgrading from OpenCode 1 to OpenCode 2, highlighting three intentional breaking changes including a new plugin API, updated server and client contracts, and consolidated terminal client configuration. The guide advises removing any existing OpenCode 1 installations before installing version 2 and explains that most existing configurations remain compatible, with optional migration to the new native V2 format. The migration process allows users to keep their current configurations and file-based definitions while gradually porting plugins and integrations to the new APIs. OpenCode 2 supports reading V1 configuration files without rewriting them, and offers tools to convert configurations to the new format when ready. Changes to permission structures, sharing policies, and agent definitions are also detailed to help users adapt their setups smoothly.

item.title: The Atlantic examines challenges and regulatory issues surrounding AI programming and big tech
item.description: The Atlantic published an article discussing the complexities and potential pitfalls of AI programming, focusing on the role of big tech companies and the need for regulatory oversight. The piece explores how AI coding impacts the technology landscape and raises concerns about governance and ethical considerations. It highlights ongoing debates about how to manage AI development responsibly amid rapid technological advances.

item.title: Microsoft plans to scale its Azure Maia AI chips to multi-gigawatt levels by 2027 as primary inference system [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Microsoft intends to deploy its in-house Azure Maia AI chips at multi-gigawatt scale starting in 2027, making them the main inference system across its products. The Maia 200 chip currently supports Microsoft Copilot in several regions, while the upcoming Maia 300 chip aims to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPUs and will target long inputs, fast chats, and agentic tasks. CEO Satya Nadella described this initiative as the company's biggest investment in its own silicon to date. Microsoft claims the Maia chips handle various AI models efficiently, pushing up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt than leading GPUs in Teams, with a 96-chip rack of Maia 300 expected to produce up to seven times the tokens of a Maia 200 rack. More technical details are expected at Ignite 2026.

item.title: Pirate Face launches a BitTorrent-based tool to decentralize Hugging Face model downloads without code changes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Pirate Face has introduced a tool that enables downloading Hugging Face models and related resources via BitTorrent, aiming to speed up distribution through peer-to-peer sharing. The tool integrates seamlessly with existing Hugging Face APIs and caches, verifying file integrity before use and falling back to standard Hugging Face servers if needed. The solution requires minimal setup, involving a single package installation and no code modifications, and supports various Hugging Face download methods including transformers and diffusers. It operates by intercepting file requests and sourcing them from a torrent swarm, ensuring compatibility and reliability while decentralizing model distribution.

item.title: Precision Numerics releases Boole-1.7B, a 1-bit language model that outperforms Bonsai-1.7B with 13.9× smaller weight storage [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Precision Numerics has introduced Boole-1.7B, a 1-bit large language model derived from Qwen3-1.7B, which achieves 85.9% of the BF16 baseline's average benchmark score while reducing stored weight size by 13.9 times. Boole-1.7B surpasses the binary Bonsai-1.7B model in seven out of ten tasks, particularly in math and code benchmarks, despite the challenges of 1-bit quantization and shared scale storage overhead. The model stores weights in 247 MB and balances the trade-offs of 1-bit quantization, where weights are represented by signs and shared magnitudes, limiting precision but greatly reducing storage. Compared to other small language models under 3 GB, Boole-1.7B offers the highest benchmark average at its storage size or below, with only ternary Bonsai-1.7B achieving a slightly higher score at nearly twice the storage size. This release highlights advances in efficient model quantization for compact language models.

Ambi's apps are available on iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch, aiming to capture context throughout the day and assist users by integrating calendar, knowledge bases, and web data. Ambi plans to expand its capabilities with a desktop app that monitors user activity for personalized suggestions and a hardware device equipped with a screen, speaker, camera, and microphones. The company emphasizes user control over ambient data capture, which is off by default, and acknowledges ongoing industry challenges around privacy and disclosure of recording to third parties.

item.title: Kevin Kelly's 2016 AI predictions foresee Google shifting from search to AI as its main product by 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Kevin Kelly's 2016 book The Inevitable predicted that by 2026, Google's primary product would transition from search to AI, driven by the company's acquisitions and integration of AI technologies. Kelly highlighted Google's use of search data to train its AI systems, suggesting that user interactions help improve Google's deep-learning models over time. Kelly also anticipated the dominance of a few large cloud-based AI providers and the rise of specialized AI software. He reflected on a 2002 conversation with Google cofounder Larry Page, who described Google as "really making an AI," emphasizing the company's long-term focus on AI development beyond search. These predictions align with Google's strategic moves and statements from CEO Sundar Pichai about AI transforming all of Google's products.

item.title: Amazon's Bargains Include Its Stock [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: It's the quiet before the storm of earnings season, which starts in a week or two. While we wait for the third-quarter updates, here's a thought: Investor enthusiasm for semiconductor stocks and blue-sky vision companies like SpaceX appears to have sucked money out of stocks of long-established tech companies. Some are now trading at bargain-basement prices. We're thinking specifically of Amazon, whose stock really deserves a bit more love. We know the gripes: Like Alphabet and Meta, Amazon is spending an absolute ton-$220 billion this year alone-on capital expenditures to build out its AI data center capacity. That's not without risk, for sure: The investment depends on business demand for AI services taking off. Even so, that can't justify Amazon trading at a discount to Walmart, as it has done for the last 18 months or so. Walmart is expected to grow revenue this year by about 5.6%-about a third of Amazon's estimated growth rate. And yet Amazon is trading at about 29 times forward earnings, compared with 37 times for Walmart, according to Koyfin data.

item.title: Zuckerberg's Big Biotech Moment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: • The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp • Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Bram Stoker's Dracula," "The AGI Chronicles" and "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched. That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code-the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: "We are learning the language in which God created life." So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies. Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. "We got a lot of eye rolls," Zuckerberg said. "People thought that was kind of crazy." Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, "That no longer seems quite so crazy." He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive "AI-powered biology." Biohub, which launched what it calls the "Virtual Biology Initiative" in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million. "We were inspired by the Human Genome Project," Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative "will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been." (Anyone going to The Information's WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.) Despite the evening's focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity-and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?) Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities. He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google's Sergey Brin, Oracle's Larry Ellison and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher. Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries. A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it's only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick. I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. "It really is a cultural moment," she said.-Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Shroud of Secrecy Cloaks Star Investor Behind Cognition, Ramp While an air of mystery hangs around Zach Frankel, he has picked up stakes in some of tech's buzziest companies and established an extensive web of connections. The GPUs in the Wine Cellar Techies are tricking out their homes with powerful AI computers. Then come the heat issues. Listening: "Bram Stoker's Dracula" How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker's classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible's new adaptation of "Dracula," Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from "Fallout" and "Yellowjackets") is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker's original from hapless victim into the story's central protagonist. Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's "Pet Sematary." -Abram Brown Reading: "The AGI Chronicles" by Kevin Roose How exactly did we get here-to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that's to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they're actually going to end all of us humans. A rather definitive answer to that question lies in "The AGI Chronicles," a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry's rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, "the strangest decade in our history." Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something "between a pipe dream and a fantasy," he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle's Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos's Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the "Stargate" TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google's Gemini was almost called Titan-a Hassabis suggestion-but company lawyers vetoed the name as "too aggressive." And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their "personal advisory council," as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) From "The AGI Chronicles," what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It's not as if they'll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him-that they "missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible," he writes. "Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought."-A.B. Watching: "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" By actor Mahershala Ali's own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel's decision to shelve his reboot of "Blade," its half-vampire vampire slayer. "I think in some ways I'm probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I've begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business," Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." "It's like you're fighting with people to see you how you see yourself." I can see how Ali's own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might've fueled his interest in doing "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges-as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who'd been attached to helm the "Blade" reboot with Ali. If nothing else, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" is a sharp jab to Marvel's ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would've made a terrific "Blade" together.-A.B.

item.title: GPUs in the Wine Cellar: Why Techies Are Hoarding AI Compute in Their Homes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The basement of Gary Flake's contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you'd expect in a multipurpose man cave. There's a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame. Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain-part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month. That's true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. "I want to own," said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. "I don't want to rent."
